sections.heading: The price drop that changes the math

image.alt: Infographic comparing AI model costs: a single dime versus a tall stack of coins
image.caption: A dime now buys an AI that reads five novels. Route the routine work there.

paragraphs: Anthropic's smallest model, Claude Haiku 5.5, got a major upgrade this week. It now costs 10 cents per million input tokens, matching OpenAI's GPT 6 Luna to the penny. Anthropic says the average job runs about 75 percent cheaper than the last Haiku, and up to 90 percent cheaper on short requests. They also halved the price of Sonnet 5.5's cache reads.

For scale, a million tokens is roughly the first five Harry Potter books. A dime now buys an AI that reads all five. The takeaway for founders: routine AI work no longer has to cost real money. It can cost pennies, as long as you route it to the right model.

sections.heading: The workflow: a manager and an assistant

image.alt: Workflow graphic showing a large manager model routing task cards to a small fast helper model
image.caption: The strong model directs. The fast model executes.

paragraphs: The Rundown AI laid out the playbook this week, and it is the same pattern I use with my own team: the strong model directs, the fast model executes.
The setup works like this:
1. Open a clean practice folder with sample tasks, like sorting customer messages into categories, and define which cases need a human's review.
2. Keep Sonnet as your main model. Ask it to create a Haiku helper that reads the task and suggests routes, without editing files or contacting anyone.
3. Have the helper sort one small batch. Verify every item appears once, with a quote from its source so you can check its work.
4. Give Sonnet only the flagged messages and their original text. Ask for review notes. Leave refunds, replies, and account changes to a person.
5. Compare the result with a Sonnet only run. Count errors, editing time, and usage across both stages before choosing which approach to keep.
Pro tip: start with one helper for a small batch rather than one agent per message. You can always scale up once the pattern works.

sections.heading: Where I would use this tomorrow
paragraphs: Sorting inbound DMs and lead messages by intent: buyer, collaborator, fan, spam. Review the flagged ones yourself. That is a daily task every growing creator has.
Categorizing expenses and receipts at the end of the week, with a human check on anything unusual.
Drafting first pass captions, outreach lists, and hashtag sets, then applying my own quality filter before anything ships. Remember the slop grenade rule: the model drafts, you direct.

excerpt: Every creator has googled the best time to post on Instagram. The charts are not lying, they are just not about your audience. Here is what actually moves reach, and how to find your real posting window.

image.alt: Large clock face with blurred hands in front of a glowing smartphone showing a social feed, purple and magenta accents
image.subject: Posting times and audience habits

sections.heading: The question every creator asks
paragraphs: Every creator has googled it. Best time to post on Instagram. You get a neat little chart that says Tuesday at 11 AM and Friday at 7 PM, and you schedule your best work into those slots, and then nothing changes.
I respect the instinct. You want every advantage. But I am going to give you the honest version that the charts leave out, because the truth will actually help you more than the chart.

sections.heading: Why the universal best time lists are mostly useless

image.alt: Two clocks side by side: one showing a single fixed time, the other surrounded by scattered activity dots at many hours
image.caption: The internet's answer is one fixed time. Your audience lives at many.

paragraphs: Those charts are built from aggregate data across millions of accounts. Your account is not an aggregate. Your audience has its own habits, its own timezone spread, its own scrolling patterns.

A chart that says post at 11 AM assumes your followers are all in one timezone, all on the same schedule, all interested in the same thing. For a music artist whose fans span three continents, that assumption falls apart immediately. For a local business whose customers are all in one city, it might be close, but close is not the same as correct.

Here is the deeper problem. The charts measure when people are online, not when they engage with your content. Being online and caring about your post are two completely different things. A million people scrolling at lunch does you no good if none of them stop for a music video clip.
So treat the charts as a starting guess, never as a strategy.

sections.heading: What actually matters more than timing
paragraphs: Three things beat posting time every single time. Learn these and the clock becomes a footnote.

sections.heading: Your niche and your audience's real habits
paragraphs: A fitness coach and a music producer do not share an audience schedule. The coach's followers scroll before work and after dinner. The producer's followers are night owls who live in the studio until 3 AM.

Think about who follows you and when they actually have attention to give. Parents scroll during nap time and after bedtime. Students scroll between classes. Service workers scroll on breaks. Your audience has a rhythm. Learn it instead of borrowing someone else's.
The fastest way to learn it is to ask. Poll your stories. When do you usually scroll? People answer these, and the answers are more accurate than any chart.

sections.heading: Algorithm training beats timing
paragraphs: This is the part nobody talks about. Instagram learns what your account is about and who should see it based on patterns in your content and your audience's behavior over weeks, not minutes.

When you post consistently about one topic, in one format, to one audience, the algorithm gets confident about who to show your work to. That confidence matters more than whether you posted at 11 AM or 2 PM. A well trained account posting at a bad time will outperform a confused account posting at the perfect time.
Training happens through repetition. Same niche, same format family, same posting rhythm. Every post teaches the system. Random posting unteaches it.

sections.heading: Consistency beats optimization
paragraphs: I would rather you post every day at a random time than post twice a week at the mathematically perfect time. Volume of reps is what builds skill, builds audience, and builds algorithmic confidence.

Creators who obsess over timing usually do it to avoid the real work, which is posting enough to get good. The perfect time to post is less important than having something worth posting. Get the reps in first. Optimize later.

sections.heading: Honest posting windows: starting points, not gospel
paragraphs: I said the charts are a starting guess. Here is mine, framed honestly as exactly that. Use these to begin, then adjust based on your own data.

sections.heading: For music artists
paragraphs: Evenings and late nights tend to work because your audience listens to music as a wind down activity. Try 7 PM to 11 PM in your primary timezone. Friday and Saturday evenings are strong because new music energy peaks on weekends. If your audience is global, pick the timezone where most of your followers live and optimize for them.

One specific tip for artists. Post your teaser content two to three hours before your audience's peak scrolling time, not during it. This gives the post time to gather early engagement so it is already moving when the big wave arrives.

sections.heading: For creators and coaches
paragraphs: Midday and early evening tend to work because your audience consumes educational content during breaks and after work. Try 11 AM to 1 PM and 6 PM to 8 PM. Weekday mornings also perform well for business minded audiences who plan their day early.
The pattern here is attention availability. Post when your specific people have a gap, not when a chart says the whole internet is awake.

sections.heading: How to find your time

image.alt: Phone screen showing an audience activity chart across 24 hours with one peak window highlighted in purple
image.caption: Your data beats every chart.

paragraphs: Open Instagram Insights on your profile. Go to your audience section and look at the most active times. Instagram shows you when your followers are online by day and hour. This data beats every chart on the internet because it is about your actual people.

Then run a simple test. Post at three different times across two weeks, keeping the content quality equal. Compare reach and saves, not just likes. Saves tell you the content was valuable enough to keep. After two weeks you will have your answer, and it will be yours, not borrowed.

sections.heading: What to do instead of chasing the perfect time
paragraphs: If you take one thing from this post, take this. The creators who win on Instagram are not the ones with the best schedule. They are the ones with the clearest niche, the most consistent output, and the deepest understanding of their specific audience.

Pick a reasonable window from the starting points above. Post there consistently for a month. Watch your own Insights. Adjust once based on real data. Then stop thinking about timing and put that energy into making the content better.

The algorithm rewards accounts it understands. It understands accounts that show up, stay on topic, and serve one audience well. Timing is a multiplier on that foundation. Without the foundation, there is nothing to multiply.

sections.heading: Your move
paragraphs: Check your Insights today and note your audience's three most active windows. Pick one and commit to it for the next 30 days. Same niche, same format family, steady rhythm. That is the whole strategy.

And if you want help making the content itself worth stopping for, start with my breakdown of reels hooks that stop the scroll in two seconds. Pair strong hooks with consistent timing and you have a system, not a superstition.

sections.heading: Why your stack matters more than your idea
paragraphs: Every founder obsesses over the idea. Almost none obsess over the stack, the nine or so tools that handle email, marketing, hosting, analytics, building, payroll, banking, and payments. The idea gets you excited. The stack gets you paid.

I saw a reel breaking down nine must have tools for founders and it was too good not to test against my own business. So I researched every one, checked the free tiers, found the referral programs, and decided which ones are actually worth setting up. Here is the full breakdown, with my honest take on each.

sections.heading: Get found and stay in touch

image.alt: Email marketing dashboard with subscriber graphs on a laptop
image.caption: Email is still the highest return channel you own. Start the list now.

paragraphs: Loops handles your email. Marketing emails, product updates, and transactional emails all in one tool, with a clean editor and a real API from day one. The free tier covers 1,000 contacts and 4,000 sends per rolling 30 days, no credit card required. Every feature ships on free, including the API and automations. You only pay when your list grows, starting at 49 dollars a month for 5,000 contacts.

My take: I have 120 blog posts and no email list tool. That is leaving money on the table. Loops is the one I am setting up first, because every visitor who leaves without subscribing is a visitor I have to earn all over again.

Mango SEO AI handles programmatic SEO. It generates content at scale with built in programmatic SEO for every keyword you target, aimed at small businesses and entrepreneurs who want first page rankings without hiring an agency. If you have a content library like mine, a tool like this multiplies what every post can do.
My take: worth testing once the email engine is running. SEO compounds, but email pays this month.

sections.heading: See what your visitors actually do

image.alt: Product analytics dashboard with charts and session replays
image.caption: Guessing what visitors do is expensive. Watching is free.

paragraphs: PostHog is product analytics, session replay, feature flags, surveys, and error tracking in one SDK. The free tier is genuinely generous: 1 million analytics events per month, 5,000 session replays, 1 million feature flag requests, plus free allowances across surveys, error tracking, and more. Over 90 percent of PostHog users never pay anything. It is also open source, so you can self host if you want full control.
My take: installing this on the site this week. I want to see where visitors drop off, which blog posts convert, and whether anyone actually clicks the booking buttons. Data beats opinions.

sections.heading: Ship without a dev team
paragraphs: Railway handles deployment. Connect your GitHub repo and it figures out the rest, no Dockerfile required. Pricing is usage based and billed by the second. New accounts start with a 5 dollar trial credit, then a free plan with a small monthly allowance. A lightweight app can run for a few dollars a month.

My take: my site runs on Cloudflare Workers and my developer handles infrastructure, so I am skipping Railway for now. If you are shipping your own app with no backend team, this is the fastest path from repo to live URL.

Claude is your frontend builder. Paired with the right skills, it produces interfaces that look expensive instead of generic. I covered the 10 Claude skills that make apps look premium in a separate post, start there if you want the full setup.

Codex is your backend builder. In the reel this means the AI coding agent for backend work. In my world it is funnier than that, because the developer who ships my site is literally named Codex. Either way, the point stands: AI writes the boilerplate now, humans make the decisions.

sections.heading: Get paid and stay legit
paragraphs: Stripe handles payments. Free to set up, no monthly fee, you pay per transaction when money moves. This is the standard for taking card payments online, and it plugs into everything. If you sell anything on the internet, you need a Stripe account.
My take: setting this up for direct payments. The 80 dollar reels and 450 dollar event packages need a checkout that is not a DM conversation. Stripe is that checkout.

Mercury handles business banking. Zero monthly fees, zero minimum balance, FDIC insured up to 5 million through partner banks, built for startups and online businesses. The referral program pays 250 dollars to both sides when a new account deposits 10,000 within 90 days. You will need your EIN, company formation documents, and a government ID to open an account.
My take: on the list once the EIN paperwork is sorted. Free business banking with no fees is a no brainer, and the referral program is real affiliate income once I am in.

Gusto handles payroll and HR. The referral program is strong, referrers earn up to 800 dollars in Visa gift cards per successful referral and the new customer gets 100 dollars after running their first payroll. But payroll software with no employees is a solution without a problem.
My take: bookmarked for the day I hire. Not a day sooner.

sections.heading: My actual stack: what I use and what is next
paragraphs: Honesty matters more than a list. Here is where I actually stand on all nine. Already in use: Claude for site work and content, and my developer Codex on infrastructure. Setting up this week: Loops for email, PostHog for analytics, Stripe for payments. Queued behind paperwork: Mercury for business banking. Testing later: Mango SEO AI for the blog library. Skipped for now: Railway because my hosting is handled, and Gusto because I have no employees yet.
The pattern is simple. Revenue tools first, vanity tools never. Email and payments put money in the account this month. Analytics tells me what to fix. Everything else waits its turn.

sections.heading: Your next step
paragraphs: Pick the one tool from this list that would change your revenue this month and set it up today. For most creators and solo founders, that is either email or payments. Everything else is optimization.
And if your website is the thing holding you back, that is what I build. Business websites that are clear about what you sell, who it is for, and what to do next. Check the pricing and let's talk.

sections.heading: What a Claude skill actually is
paragraphs: A Claude skill is a folder of instructions that teaches Claude how to do one job well. You install it once. After that, Claude reads it automatically whenever the task fits. No extra prompting. No pasting long instructions every time.

Think of it like hiring a specialist. You would not ask your videographer to also do your taxes. Skills give Claude that same focus. One skill for design direction. One skill for color systems. One skill for mobile layouts.

Installation takes about a minute per skill. Add it as a Claude Code plugin, pull it with npx, or copy the folder into your skills directory. Every repo is linked in the sources below so you can grab them directly.

sections.heading: Start with these two
paragraphs: Frontend Design, the official skill by Anthropic. This is the one you install first. It forces Claude to pick a real visual direction before writing a single line of code. Brutalist, editorial, retro futuristic, refined minimal. It also blocks the generic defaults that make every AI built site look the same. Same font, same gradient, same three cards. If your Claude output looks cheap, this skill is the fix.

UI UX Pro Max. This is the heavyweight. Searchable design intelligence with dozens of styles, nearly 200 product palettes, 74 font pairings, and over 100 UX guidelines. Tell it what you are building and it picks a design system that fits the product. A fintech dashboard gets a fintech system, not a generic template. image.alt: Designer reviewing app interface for quality
image.caption: Let Claude critique its own work before you ship.

paragraphs: Impeccable. Point Claude at a finished interface and get a structured critique. It reviews the work against real design principles instead of just saying it looks good. Run it after every build and your output tightens fast.

Interface Design. Focused on hierarchy and composition. It asks the right review questions. What does the eye hit first. Does the layout guide you toward the action. Keep your project design notes as the single source of truth and let this skill check new work against them.

sections.heading: The polish layer
paragraphs: Responsive Craft. Your site lives or dies on mobile. This skill checks exactly how components behave across screen widths, scrolling, keyboard states, and safe areas. It is the difference between a site that works on your laptop and a site that works everywhere.
Hue. Color systems done right. Reusable token models and component specimens so your palette stays consistent across every page. No more five slightly different purples drifting through your site.

Scroll Craft. For premium scroll driven pages. It treats motion and craft as one job instead of two. The skill ships with worked examples of real approved sites so you can see the quality bar before you build.

Epic Design and Mobile App UI Design round out the ten. Epic Design focuses on cinematic scrolled layouts. Mobile App UI Design covers native feeling mobile patterns. paragraphs: Zuckerberg's pitch: the full Muse experience on a keychain, including the real-time voice and avatar stack. If you are not wearing smart glasses, the Charm is the fastest way to talk to your Muse and show it what is going on around you. Muse runs in a dedicated cloud virtual machine and keeps working on longer tasks after you walk away, asking approval before purchases. The Charm is the pager for that agent: hand over a task by voice, let it see the scene, approve or reject what it wants to do next. It does not do phone or video calls.
